[Metropolitan France](/wiki/Metropolitan_France "Metropolitan France") shares borders with [Belgium](/wiki/Belgium "Belgium") and [Luxembourg](/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg") to the north; [Germany](/wiki/Germany "Germany") to the northeast; [Switzerland](/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") to the east; [Italy](/wiki/Italy "Italy") and [Monaco](/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") to the southeast; [Andorra](/wiki/Andorra "Andorra") and [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain") to the south; and a maritime border with the [United Kingdom](/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") to the northwest. Its metropolitan area extends from the [Rhine](/wiki/Rhine "Rhine") to the [Atlantic Ocean](/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") and from the [Mediterranean Sea](/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") to the [English Channel](/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") and the [North Sea](/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea"). Its 18 [integral regions](/wiki/Regions_of_France "Regions of France")—five of which are overseas—span a combined area of 632,702 km2 (244,288 sq mi), with [a total population](/wiki/Demographics_of_France "Demographics of France") estimated at over 69.1 million in 2026.

**René François Armand** "**Sully**" **Prudhomme** (French: [[syli pʁydɔm]](/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); 16 March 1839 – 6 September 1907) was a French poet and essayist. He was the first winner of the [Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1901](/wiki/1901_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1901 Nobel Prize in Literature").

Born in Paris, Prudhomme originally studied to be an engineer, but turned to philosophy and later to poetry; he declared it as his intention to create scientific poetry for modern times. In character sincere and melancholic, he was linked to the [Parnassus school](/wiki/Parnassianism "Parnassianism"), although, at the same time, his work displays characteristics of its own.

[Floristically](/wiki/Floristics "Floristics"), the Sahara has three zones based on the amount of rainfall received – the Northern (Mediterranean), Central and Southern Zones. There are two transitional zones – the Mediterranean-Sahara transition and the Sahel transition zone.[[50]](#cite_note-Mares1999-50)

The Saharan flora comprises around 2800 species of [vascular plants](/wiki/Vascular_plant "Vascular plant"). Approximately a quarter of these are [endemic](/wiki/Endemism "Endemism"). About half of these species are common to the flora of the Arabian deserts.[[51]](#cite_note-Houérou2008-51)

Between 1942 and 1945, there were four main [areas of conflict](/wiki/Theater_(military) "Theater (military)") in the Pacific War: China, the [Central Pacific](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean_theater_of_World_War_II "Pacific Ocean theater of World War II"), [South-East Asia](/wiki/South-East_Asian_theatre_of_World_War_II "South-East Asian theatre of World War II") and the [South West Pacific](/wiki/South_West_Pacific_theatre_of_World_War_II "South West Pacific theatre of World War II"). US sources refer to two theaters within the Pacific War: the Pacific theater and the [China Burma India Theater](/wiki/China_Burma_India_Theater_of_World_War_II "China Burma India Theater of World War II") (CBI). However, these were not operational commands.

In the Pacific, the Allies divided operational control of their forces between two supreme commands, known as [Pacific Ocean Areas](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean_Areas_(command) "Pacific Ocean Areas (command)") and [Southwest Pacific Area](/wiki/South_West_Pacific_Area_(command) "South West Pacific Area (command)").[[55]](#cite_note-63)

The [Imperial Japanese Navy](/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Navy_in_World_War_II "Imperial Japanese Navy in World War II") (IJN) did not integrate its units into permanent theater commands. The [Imperial Japanese Army](/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Army "Imperial Japanese Army") (IJA), which had already created the [Kwantung Army](/wiki/Kwantung_Army "Kwantung Army") to oversee its occupation of Manchukuo and the [China Expeditionary Army](/wiki/China_Expeditionary_Army "China Expeditionary Army") during the Second Sino-Japanese War, created the [Southern Expeditionary Army Group](/wiki/Southern_Expeditionary_Army_Group "Southern Expeditionary Army Group") at the outset of its conquests of South East Asia. This headquarters controlled the bulk of the Japanese Army formations which opposed the Western Allies in the Pacific and South East Asia.

On August 17, Phelps won his eighth gold medal in the 4×100-meter medley relay, breaking [Mark Spitz](/wiki/Mark_Spitz "Mark Spitz")'s record of seven gold medals won in a single Olympic Games, which had stood since 1972.[[160]](#cite_note-Phelps,_No_Limits,_p._218-160) Phelps, along with teammates [Brendan Hansen](/wiki/Brendan_Hansen "Brendan Hansen"), [Aaron Peirsol](/wiki/Aaron_Peirsol "Aaron Peirsol"), and Jason Lezak, set a new world record in the event with a time of 3 minutes and 29.34 seconds, 0.7 seconds ahead of second-place Australia and 1.34 seconds faster than the previous record set by the United States at the 2004 Olympic Games in Athens. When Phelps dived in to swim the 100-meter butterfly leg, the third leg of the 400-meter medley, the United States had been trailing Australia and Japan. Phelps completed his split in 50.1 seconds, the fastest butterfly split ever for the event, giving teammate Jason Lezak a more than half-second lead for the final leg, which he held onto to clinch the event in world record time.[[161]](#cite_note-161) Said Phelps, upon completing the event that awarded him his eighth gold medal and eighth Olympic record in as many events, "Records are always made to be broken no matter what they are ... Anybody can do anything that they set their mind to."[[162]](#cite_note-162)
